extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers / readers of Montaigne (early-modern moralist essays)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading / normative reflections in a Montaigne-style essay about horsemanship, ancient customs, judgment, rhetoric, and human manners; mixes anecdote, moralising, and examples to state evaluative principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good horseman / horsemanship
rubrics_metrics.description: A good horseman... seems rather to have respect to the courage of the man than address in riding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises practical skill: "the most knowing in that art, who had the best seat and the best method in breaking horses, was Monsieur de Carnavalet"; examples of skilled feats (riding with feet on saddle, re-saddling at full gallop, shooting backwards) illustrate exemplary horsemanship as a combination of seat, control, and daring practical ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an 'entire' horse
rubrics_metrics.description: We call a horse entire, that has his mane and ears so, and no other will pass muster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as a standard for judging a horse's completeness or suitability; followed by historical note that Lacedaemonians shorn captured horses in triumph (an example of judging/marking horses by this standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let custom blind your judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: I find fault with their singular indiscretion in suffering themselves to be so blinded and imposed upon by the authority of the present usage as every month to alter their opinion, if custom so require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns against accepting current fashions or usages as the sole pattern of perfection; he advises recalling old customs to steady judgment and condemns fickle changes in taste (e.g., shifting fashions of dress) as a moral failing of judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the limits of your judgement (intellectual humility)
rubrics_metrics.description: This knowledge that a man can proceed no further, is one effect of its virtue... finding it too deep for my stature, I keep me on the shore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne explicitly endorses recognising when a subject is beyond one's competence: sound judgement includes the restraint to stay within one's intellectual reach rather than overreaching and risking error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character is revealed in every small employment or diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Every particle, every employment of man manifests him equally with any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small acts and pastimes (e.g., playing chess) as reliable indicators of character and passions; the essay argues one learns as much about a man's soul from trivial pursuits as from great actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer laughter/jeering over sorrow in judging human folly
rubrics_metrics.description: I am clearly for the first humour [laughing];... because it expresses more contempt and condemnation than the other, and I think we can never be despised according to our full desert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that laughing at human absurdity denotes contempt (showing the thing is of no moment), whereas weeping implies undue esteem; he cites Democritus (laughing) as a wiser stance than Timon (weeping). This is a recommended stance for moral evaluation of human folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric is primarily a tool of persuasion and can be deceptive
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristo wisely defined rhetoric to be 'a science to persuade the people;' Socrates and Plato 'an art to flatter and deceive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne treats rhetoric with suspicion: it is 'an engine invented to manage and govern a disorderly and tumultuous rabble' and flourishes where public affairs are in commotion. The guidance is to distrust eloquence that aims to move affections rather than discover truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid striving for greatness in frivolous matters
rubrics_metrics.description: to be eminent, to excel above the common rate in frivolous things, nowise befits a man of honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the chess example: summoning all faculties for a trivial game is a misplacement of ambition; excellence should not be sought in matters unworthy of great concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adulterate the essence of things with deceptive appearances or inflated language
rubrics_metrics.description: They would... make profession of a tricky and deceitful act... to deceive not our sight only but our judgments, and to adulterate and corrupt the very essence of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticises both painters who plaster up their beauty and rhetoricians who use lofty words to distort reality; the implicit standard is to value truthfulness of substance over cosmetic or linguistic artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve great surnames and honors for truly exceptional persons
rubrics_metrics.description: we... unworthily and indifferently... confer upon any we think fit the most glorious surnames with which antiquity honoured but one or two persons in several ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne objects to casual bestowal of exalted titles (e.g., calling Aretin 'divine' as Plato was); the guidance is to apply terms of highest praise sparingly and only when merited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony (frugality) as a mark of virtue in public men
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: the elder Cato sold his warhorse to save its carriage cost; Scipio Aemilianus travelled with only seven servants; Homer had one, Plato three, Zeno none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne presents historical exemplars to recommend parsimonious living for statesmen and men of consequence, implying modest private expense as a standard of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete, practical examples rather than bombast to judge specialized professions
rubrics_metrics.description: When I hear our architects thunder out their bombast words... my imagination is presently possessed with the palace of Apollidon; when, after all, I find them but the paltry pieces of my own kitchen door.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of technical jargon used to impress; prefer assessing professional competence by observable practical outcomes rather than by impressive-sounding terminology.
